concept.name: DDD Tactical Patterns

relationships.description: Connects DDD Tactical Patterns to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Building-block patterns—Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, Domain Events, and Repositories—that encapsulate business invariants inside clear transactional consistency boundaries.
spark.keyTakeaway: Design small Aggregates around true atomic invariants, reference other Aggregates by ID rather than object graph, and coordinate cross-Aggregate side effects via Domain Events.

concept.whyItMatters: In anemic domain models, business rules scatter across controllers, service classes, and SQL triggers, making it easy for concurrent requests to violate invariants—such as double-spending a wallet balance or confirming an order whose total exceeds a credit limit. DDD tactical patterns concentrate those invariants inside cohesive Aggregates protected by optimistic locking, so invalid state transitions become impossible to persist.
whenToUse: Core domain workflows with complex state machines, multi-field invariants, and concurrent updates (e.g., order fulfillment, ledger postings, seat reservations).
Systems where business rules change frequently and need fast, deterministic unit tests without spinning up a database.
Services transitioning away from anemic getter/setter entities where validation logic is duplicated across multiple endpoints.
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD admin screens, CMS content tables, or reporting dashboards with no invariants beyond basic field validation.
High-throughput analytical ingestion pipelines where row-by-row object hydration would bottleneck batch throughput.
Read-heavy query paths (better served by CQRS read projections or direct SQL/DTO queries bypassing Aggregates).
keyPoints: Entities have a continuous identity (`OrderId`, `AccountId`) across state mutations; Value Objects (`Money`, `DateRange`, `EmailAddress`) are immutable, side-effect-free, and compared purely by their attributes.
An Aggregate is a cluster of Entities and Value Objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with one Aggregate Root controlling all external access and enforcing invariants.
Keep Aggregates small: reference other Aggregates exclusively by ID (`customerId: CustomerId`) rather than lazy-loaded ORM object graphs to avoid massive lock contention and N+1 queries.
Each transaction should modify at most one Aggregate instance; use Domain Events (`OrderPaid`, `InventoryReserved`) with an outbox table for eventual consistency across Aggregates.
Repositories abstract persistence at the Aggregate Root level (`findById`, `save`), never exposing arbitrary child-entity queries or leaking ORM session mechanics into domain logic.

examples.title: Preventing negative wallet balance with an Aggregate Root
examples.scenario: A fintech wallet service previously used an anemic `Wallet` entity with `setBalance()`, allowing two concurrent `POST /withdraw` requests to both read ₹1,000 and write ₹200.
examples.outcome: Refactoring `Wallet` into an Aggregate Root with `withdraw(Money amount)` and a `@Version` optimistic lock column enforces `balance >= amount` atomically, rejecting the second concurrent request with `OptimisticLockException`.

examples.title: Immutable Money Value Object eliminating currency bugs
examples.scenario: An international marketplace passed raw `BigDecimal` amounts and separate `String currency` parameters across 14 services, causing a bug where EUR and USD amounts were summed directly.
examples.outcome: Introducing an immutable `Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency)` Value Object that throws `CurrencyMismatchException` on `add()` caught currency bugs at unit-test and runtime boundaries.

tradeOffs.factor: Small Aggregates vs. Large Object Graphs
tradeOffs.pro: Small Aggregates (e.g., `Order` + `OrderLines` only) minimize optimistic-lock collisions and keep hydration fast.
tradeOffs.con: Cross-aggregate rules (e.g., updating `Customer.totalSpent` when an `Order` closes) become eventually consistent via Domain Events.

tradeOffs.factor: Rich Domain Model vs. Anemic Transaction Script
tradeOffs.pro: Business invariants live in one testable place and cannot be bypassed by callers.
tradeOffs.con: Higher upfront design effort and ORM mapping friction (e.g., JPA private constructors, embedded value objects).

tradeOffs.factor: Domain Events via Outbox vs. Synchronous Service Calls
tradeOffs.pro: Outbox-backed Domain Events decouple side effects (email, loyalty points) from the core commit path.
tradeOffs.con: Requires idempotent consumers and monitoring for outbox relay lag.

failureModes.name: God Aggregate contention
failureModes.description: Modeling `Customer` as an Aggregate containing all `Orders`, `Invoices`, and `Tickets` causes every checkout and support ticket update to collide on the same `Customer` row version.
failureModes.mitigation: Split `Customer`, `Order`, and `Ticket` into separate Aggregates linked only by `customerId`.

failureModes.name: Missing optimistic concurrency control
failureModes.description: Two threads load the same `InventoryItem` Aggregate, both pass the `stock >= qty` check in memory, and the second `save()` silently overwrites the first.
failureModes.mitigation: Add a monotonically increasing `version` column (`WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`) on every Aggregate Root table.

failureModes.name: Lost Domain Events on dual-write
failureModes.description: Publishing a Domain Event to Kafka after `repository.save()` fails if the process crashes between the DB commit and the Kafka `send()`, leaving downstream Aggregates out of sync.
failureModes.mitigation: Persist Domain Events into a local `outbox` table inside the exact same DB transaction as the Aggregate.

failureModes.name: Anemic Aggregate with public setters
failureModes.description: Exposing `order.setStatus(CANCELLED)` lets callers skip refund checks or `OrderCancelled` event emission.
failureModes.mitigation: Make setters private/package-private and expose intention-revealing methods (`order.cancel(reason, clock)`).

commonMistakes: Creating a Repository for every child table (`OrderLineRepository`) instead of only for Aggregate Roots (`OrderRepository`).
Using database-generated auto-increment IDs that are null until `save()`, forcing persistence calls before domain logic can reference the entity's ID.
Injecting HTTP clients, repositories, or Kafka producers directly into Domain Entities instead of keeping Aggregates pure and orchestrating I/O in Application Services.
Overusing Value Objects without overriding equality (`equals`/`hashCode` or Python `@dataclass(frozen=True)`), breaking set/map lookups.
Applying heavy tactical DDD ceremony (factories, specifications, domain services) to simple read-only reporting endpoints that should just run a SQL projection.

sections.content:
## The idea

Tactical DDD organizes domain code around **consistency boundaries** rather than database tables. Instead of exposing raw data records with public setters, you model behavior and invariants directly on domain types:

- **Value Objects** (`Money`, `Address`, `OrderLineQuantity`) are immutable, self-validating, and interchangeable when their attributes match.
- **Entities** (`Order`, `Shipment`) carry a stable identity (`UUIDv7` or domain ID) across their lifecycle.
- **Aggregates** group an Entity root with its tightly coupled child entities/value objects that *must* change together atomically. All external code interacts only with the **Aggregate Root**, which guarantees invariants on every method call and persists atomically via a **Repository**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an `Order` Aggregate handling item additions and checkout confirmation:

1. **Command arrives**: Application service receives `ConfirmOrderCommand(orderId, paymentId)`.
2. **Hydrate Aggregate**: `OrderRepository.findById(orderId)` loads the `Order` root, its `OrderLine` items, and its `version = 4` from PostgreSQL.
3. **Enforce invariants in memory**: `order.confirm(paymentId, now)` checks that `status == DRAFT`, `lines.size() > 0`, and `total.isPositive()`. It transitions `status = CONFIRMED` and records an internal `OrderConfirmed` Domain Event.
4. **Atomic persistence + Outbox**: `OrderRepository.save(order)` executes `UPDATE orders SET status = 'CONFIRMED', version = 5 WHERE id = ? AND version = 4` and inserts `OrderConfirmed` into `outbox_events` within one ACID transaction.
5. **Eventual consistency**: An outbox relay publishes `OrderConfirmed` to Kafka so `Inventory` and `Billing` Aggregates react asynchronously.

sections.content:
## Sizing Aggregates & cross-Aggregate coordination

Vaughn Vernon's rule of thumb for Aggregate design is: **protect true invariants in consistency boundaries, and design small Aggregates**. Only put two entities in the same Aggregate if a business rule *immediately* breaks unless both change in the same ACID commit (e.g., `Order` total must equal the sum of its `OrderLine` subtotals).

If a rule can tolerate 100ms–2s of delay (e.g., updating a `Customer`'s loyalty tier after an order ships), keep them in separate Aggregates, reference `customerId` by value, and emit a Domain Event. If a single Aggregate grows too large, concurrent users will hit `OptimisticLockException` constantly.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Tactical building blocks at a glance
sections.content:
## Tactical building blocks at a glance

| Pattern | Mutability & Identity | Responsibility | Anti-Pattern to Avoid |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Value Object** | Immutable, no ID | Encapsulates measurements, validation, math (`Money`) | Primitive obsession (`BigDecimal` + `String`) |
| **Entity** | Mutable, stable ID | Tracks lifecycle within an Aggregate (`OrderLine`) | Public setters bypassing validation |
| **Aggregate Root** | Mutable, global ID | Enforces atomic invariants, owns child entities | Embedding unrelated Aggregates by reference |
| **Domain Event** | Immutable, past-tense | Broadcasts committed state transitions (`OrderPaid`) | Dual-writing to DB and broker without Outbox |
| **Repository** | Stateless interface | Loads and saves whole Aggregate Roots (`save`) | Returning lazy-loaded ORM proxies to controllers |

## Failure modes

The most common failure is **lazy-loading leakage**: using JPA/Hibernate `@OneToMany(fetch = LAZY)` inside an Aggregate so domain methods silently trigger SQL queries or fail with `LazyInitializationException` outside the transaction.

Another failure is **Domain Services becoming procedural god-classes**: when logic that belongs on an Aggregate (`order.applyDiscount()`) is placed in `OrderDomainService`, the Aggregate reverts to an anemic data bag. Use Domain Services only for stateless operations that genuinely span multiple Aggregates (like a `CurrencyConverter` or `TransferService`).

## Testing & CQRS separation

Because Aggregates have zero dependencies on HTTP, SQL, or message brokers, you can test every edge case (`confirm()` on empty cart, double-cancellation, currency mismatch) in sub-millisecond pure unit tests.

For complex read screens (e.g., paginated order history joined with customer names and tracking status), bypass Aggregates entirely using **CQRS**: query a denormalized read view or SQL DTO projection directly, reserving Aggregates strictly for the write path.

## Practical checklist

- Model `Money`, `Email`, `DateRange`, and IDs as immutable Value Objects that validate on construction.
- Reference external Aggregates strictly by ID (`CustomerId`), never by ORM object reference.
- Include a `version` column on every Aggregate Root for optimistic concurrency control.
- Persist Domain Events in a transactional `outbox_events` table rather than dual-writing to Kafka/RabbitMQ.
- Bypass Aggregates on read-only list/search endpoints using lightweight SQL projections.

interviewProblems.title: DDD Tactical Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on DDD Tactical Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Building-block patterns—Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, Domain Events, and Repositories—that encapsulate business invariants inside clear transactional consistency boundaries.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Order Repository applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PostgreSQL + Outbox.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PostgreSQL + Outbox experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Split `Customer`, `Order`, and `Ticket` into separate Aggregates linked only by `customerId`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Design small Aggregates around true atomic invariants, reference other Aggregates by ID rather than object graph, and coordinate cross-Aggregate side effects via Domain Events.
Avoid trap: Creating a Repository for every child table (`OrderLineRepository`) instead of only for Aggregate Roots (`OrderRepository`).
Avoid trap: Using database-generated auto-increment IDs that are null until `save()`, forcing persistence calls before domain logic can reference the entity's ID.
When to reach for it: Core domain workflows with complex state machines, multi-field invariants, and concurrent updates (e.g., order fulfillment, ledger postings, seat reservations).
When to reach for it: Systems where business rules change frequently and need fast, deterministic unit tests without spinning up a database.

putItTogether.title: Putting Ddd Tactical Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Design small Aggregates around true atomic invariants, reference other Aggregates by ID rather than object graph, and coordinate cross-Aggregate side effects via Domain Events.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Ddd Tactical Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Refactoring `Wallet` into an Aggregate Root with `withdraw(Money amount)` and a `@Version` optimistic lock column enforces `balance >= amount` atomically, rejecting the second concurrent request with `OptimisticLockException`.
